messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a follow-up question regarding this original post. As a reminder, my data consist of time-of-detection data in which point counts were conducted for marsh bird species. At all fixed-area survey points (n=479), 5-min point counts were divided into 5 1-minute intervals (i.e. secondary periods) and individual detections were recorded during each minute. Each point was surveyed 3 times (i.e. 3 primary periods) during each year (there are 2 years of data).

With others' helpful advice (thanks!), I decided to stack the two years of data and use gmultimix, such that I began with a Y data structure of 479 [points]*2 [yrs] rows and 31 [possible detection histories]*3 [primary periods] columns. However, not all points were surveyed during both years or even during all 3 primary periods in a given year. Thus, I removed all rows of Y data and covariate data (e.g. date, time) that represented points which were NOT surveyed at all in a given year (i.e. rows of all NAs in date and time matrices).

Some NAs still remained in the date and time covariate matrices where a given point was not surveyed during one (or two) of the 3 primary periods, e.g. point A was only surveyed in primary periods 1 and 2, so date and time covariates would have NA in column 3. I converted these remaining NAs (10% of the data) to zero (after scaling the covariates). The models converge and estimates seem reasonable given this structure.

What I'm wondering is (which may or may not be an issue): do I need to do something else to account for the unsurveyed primary periods in regards to the encounter histories? Or is my current approach OK as is?

Hopefully my question makes sense - thanks in advance for any advice!

On Thursday, April 12, 2018 at 9:26:40 AM UTC-4, sarahps...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi John,
>
> Thanks so much for the quick response and advice - I agree that a GMM fit using gmultimix sounds like the way to go. I greatly appreciate the help!
>
> On Tuesday, April 10, 2018 at 7:33:18 PM UTC-4, John Clare wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > >
> > > 1. Is the correct data format structure: tabulated capture histories for each point count site such that I have a matrix of 479 rows by 30 columns (i.e. number of observable encounter histories from 5 time intervals)?
> >
> > 30 columns seems correct for a single-closed period. Because you have repeated visits and time-of-detection, you might choose to fit a generalized multinomial mixture (with parameters for availability and detection given availability), in which case you might want 479*2 years rows and 30*3 visits columns. If you fit a strictly closed model (say, with a call to multinomPois), I think you'd have to format this as 30 columns with 479*2*3 rows. If you want to fit a model with explicit dynamics (i.e., parameters corresponding to changes in abundance between years, or between surveys and years), you'll have to code something up. Any of these approaches might be okay, depending upon your specific objectives/foci/etc.
> >
> > > 2. Will I need to define the piFun for the time-of-detection method? Would it look like this below?
> > >
> > That pi function looks correct for a constant (M0) detection model, without looking closely to see if there are typos or missing encounter history types or anything.
> >
> >
> > > 3. Would the obsToY argument in the multinomPois function be: o2y <- matrix(1, 5, 30)?
> >
> > Depends upon how you construct the unmarked frame. The number of rows here corresponds to the number of columns in some observation covariate: for the pi function above, this argument might work if any covariate you wanted to work with relates to time interval 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. If you don't have any observation covariates, then I guess 1 row would be fine. If you stack the data and treat each site*year*visit as a separate row in the observation matrix, date and time are actually functioning as site covariates. If you have 2*497 rows and 3*30 columns in y, then I *think* (for time and date, at least) that o2y <- matrix(1, 6, 30) will work.
> >
> > >
> > > 4. In the cap-recap vignette, the time (time.1) and date (date.1) of only the first surveys of the the year were included in the siteCovs argument. However, my data consist of 3 surveys a year - how would I include time (i.e. time.1, time.2, time.3) and date (date.1, date.2, date.3) as obsCovs?
> >
> > You can do this in a gmultimix unmarked frame easily. Not in a stacked unmarked frame used to fit a strictly closed model--these, again, would be siteCovs.

Just an update that may be useful to others: I answered my own question by opting to handle NAs in a way that still allowed me to compare models using AIC. I added NAs to the Y matrix of encounter histories that corresponded to the NAs in the covariates. In this way, unmarked doesn't throw out an entire row of data (which it would do if there were NAs present in the covariates), and I don't have to impute missing covariate data with the mean of 0 (given that I had ~10% data missing from unsurveyed primary periods).

This may have been an obvious solution, but it took some extra digging in this google group to get that bolt of inspiration! And I think it makes the most sense given my data situation. This new approach for handling the unsurveyed primary periods yields very similar (but not identical) results as my previous approach of imputing missing NAs with 0 (while keeping the 0 frequencies of potential encounter histories in the Y matrix) - I imagine that's because my missing data only comprised ~10% of all observations and results would be quite different if missing data comprised >10% of the total.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrea,

this is not necessarily specific to the chi-square goodness of fit test
implemented in AICcmodavg. With a total of only 7 sites and the "rogue"
site 5 with extreme values compared to the other 6 sites, it is not
surprising to experience lack-of-fit. The test is simply saying that it
is difficult to simulate a data set with the same characteristics as
those observed in your data based on the parameters estimated in the
original model. Regarding the c-hat you report, moderate deviations
from 1 (< ~ 3 - 4) suggest that lack-of-fit is due to overdispersion,
but that the model may still be adequate. A c-hat ~ 40 (similar to the
one you report) rather suggests that the lack-of-fit observed is not
only a result of overdispersion, but that the model structure is
inappropriate.

You could set up a small simulation to see how the number of sites
influences your ability to estimate the parameters in the model and
their variance by progressively increasing the number of sites. There
are already a number of very useful resources out there to help you
through it, starting with Andy's 2004 paper (Royle, J. A. 2004. N-
mixture models for estimating population size from spatially replicated
counts. Biometrics 60:108-115), and a number of good books such as:
Kéry, M. 2010. Introduction to WinBUGS for ecologists: a Bayesian
approach to regression, ANOVA, mixed models and related analyses.
Academic Press, New York, USA.
Kéry, M., and J. A. Royle. 2016. Applied hierarchical modeling in
ecology: analysis of distribution, abundance and species richness in R
and BUGS. Academic Press, New York, USA.

Hope it helps,

messages.body_plain:
Hello every one! (apologies for cross-posting)

While you probably don't need it, you might know someone that would benefit from an introduction to R. To this effect, I present to you: "Prelude in R" (www.preludeinR.com <http://www.preludeinR.com>) (*cue shameless promo)

As you might have guessed by the name, this website is designed to give any person (students, managers, wildlife professionals, etc) the keys to start learning R, from scratch, using humor, practical examples, and exercises.
If you want to learn or progress in R, and love bad jokes and even worse puns, that's the place for you!

One of the biggest issues I've seen with introductions to R is how "dry" they can be. While effective, they can struggle to keep the reader engaged. More importantly, it can seem esoteric for someone with little to no experience in coding and stats. This is what I've tried to tackle here. An introduction in R where you can smile once in a while (if anything at how ridiculous the jokes are), while providing everything you need to start and become self-sufficient using R!

Feel free to share this website with anyone that could either get a chuckle out of it, or find it useful. If you want to use it for classes, go for it! If you find this site so beautiful you feel the irresistible need to print it on a canvas, and put it as the centerpiece in your living room... Well... Send pictures, because I'd love to see that!

If you notice errors, or important things that are missing, let me know! And I hope you'll like it!

Florent Bled

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm new to using unmarked, but was unable to find a previous post for this.

Changing the order of surveys seems to give me different estimates from the occu() function. My data has 16 surveys (undertaken by 16 different observers). When the different surveys are treated as a detection covariate, the detection estimates for each vary if the surveys are ordered differently - i.e. for the y argument in the unmarkedFrameOccu(). My data seems to be giving me a limited number of solutions. Also, when I combine with other detection covariates the occupancy estimate varies too. As I want to bootstrap my data, I want to ensure that the order won't make a difference to the estimates.

I've tried to recreate this effect by tweaking the example from the help file (code below).

Any help and advice would be greatly appreciated.

thanks
Naveed

data(frogs)

## example from help for occu()
pferUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(pfer.bin)
plot(pferUMF, panels=4)
# add some fake covariates for illustration
siteCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(sitevar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF)))
# observation covariates are in site-major, observation-minor order
obsCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(obsvar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF) * obsNum(pferUMF)))
(fm <- occu(~ obsvar1 ~ 1, pferUMF))
confint(fm, type='det', method = 'normal')
confint(fm, type='det', method = 'profile')
# estimate detection effect at obsvars=0.5
(lc <- linearComb(fm['det'],c(1,0.5)))
# transform this to probability (0 to 1) scale and get confidence limits
(btlc <- backTransform(lc))
confint(btlc, level = 0.9)
# Empirical Bayes estimates of proportion of sites occupied
re <- ranef(fm)
sum(bup(re, stat="mode"))

## changing survey order
pferUMF1 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(pfer.bin[, c(1, 3, 2)]) # change order of surveys in pfer.bin[, c(1,3,2)]
plot(pferUMF1, panels=4)
# add some fake covariates for illustration
siteCovs(pferUMF1) <- data.frame(sitevar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF1)))
# observation covariates are in site-major, observation-minor order
obsCovs(pferUMF1) <- data.frame(obsvar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF1) * obsNum(pferUMF1)))
(fm1 <- occu(~ obsvar1 ~ 1, pferUMF1))
confint(fm1, type='det', method = 'normal')
confint(fm1, type='det', method = 'profile')
# estimate detection effect at obsvars=0.5
(lc1 <- linearComb(fm1['det'],c(1,0.5)))
# transform this to probability (0 to 1) scale and get confidence limits
(btlc1 <- backTransform(lc1))
confint(btlc1, level = 0.9)
# Empirical Bayes estimates of proportion of sites occupied
re1 <- ranef(fm1)
sum(bup(re1, stat="mode"))

messages.body_plain:
aha - thank you!

For my own original data, the differing psi estimates occur when I set up the model with covariates that give poor estimates for psi, usually close to 1.0 (cf true psi = 0.6).

As you suggested, I've re-run it a few times with data to give lower psi estimates. These psi estimates are usually precisely the same, but sometimes are very slightly different (example results are below). When I use much larger numbers of surveys and sample sites, differences occur more often, but are still small.
The detection probability estimates for each observer are also very slightly different, depending on how the surveys are ordered, but the size of this is also small.

I don't think this should affect my bootstraps too much.

thanks for the help,
Naveed

obs <- function(){
  obsV <- vector(length = 180)
  for(i in 1:180) {
    if(psi[i] == 1)
      obsV[i] <- sample(c(0, 1), size = 1, prob = c(0.5, 0.5))
    else

  }
  obsV

  P_det <- c(P_det1, P_det2, P_det3, P_det4, P_det5, P_det6)
  P_est <- 1 / (1 + exp(1) ^ (-P_det))
  print(data.frame(P_est = P_est))
